input_signals.name: BalanceSheetAccrualsWhileLeveringUp
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(lt, at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accrual-inflated earnings are most dangerous in firms whose leverage has been ratcheting upward for several years, because that is where management is defending reported numbers while the balance sheet erodes; the effect should be stronger and better measured with a full-sample accrual definition.
input_signals.reasoning: This keeps the only conditioning variable that produced a reliable FF5 alpha (−3.8%/yr, t = −2.83) but replaces the cash-flow-statement accrual core with the balance-sheet construction Δ(AR+INV−AP) − depreciation, which needs no oancf and should roughly double coverage. If the alpha survives with materially higher coverage it becomes a credible result rather than a small-sample artifact, and if it collapses we learn the earlier alpha was driven by the post-1988 oancf subsample.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( trend( ratio( lt, at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualBuildAsCashCushionDrains
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, lt), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A working-capital accrual build is a cash drain; it becomes a distress signal only when the firm's cash reserves relative to its obligations are simultaneously falling, because that combination means the build is being financed out of a shrinking liquidity buffer rather than out of slack.
input_signals.reasoning: This makes the interaction contemporaneous and flow-based — accrual build meets liquidity depletion in the same year — rather than pairing a flow with a stock, which is the design flaw shared by most of the archive. It tests whether the deterioration effect in Signal 1 is really about debt or about the cash cushion being consumed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, lt ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: WorkingCapitalBuildFundedByShortDebt
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, lt), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The funding source matters: a working-capital accrual build financed by a shift toward short-maturity debt creates a maturity mismatch, since illiquid receivables and inventory are being carried on liabilities that must be rolled within the year.
input_signals.reasoning: This proposes a maturity-structure channel rather than a leverage-level or leverage-trend channel, so it is economically separable from Signals 1 and 2 even though it shares the accrual core. The conditioner is the change in the short-term share of total liabilities, which rises when banks shorten terms on weakening borrowers, making it a market-validated distress signal rather than an accounting ratio.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( delta( ratio( dlc, lt ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualBuildAfterMultiYearCashErosion
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(che, lt), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What conditions the accrual effect is a pre-existing, multi-year erosion of the cash cushion relative to obligations, not the mechanical same-year cash decline that any working-capital build must produce.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that in AccrualBuildAsCashCushionDrains the two legs are coupled through the cash-flow identity, so the winning result could be a near-quadratic in accruals rather than genuine conditioning. Replacing the contemporaneous ΔCash/LT with a three-year trend breaks the same-year accounting link while preserving the economics, so if the alpha survives the conditioning interpretation is vindicated and if it vanishes we have diagnosed the artifact.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( trend( ratio( che, lt ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ChronicAccrualStockMeetsLiquidityDrain
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), 3), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, lt), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of accrual build can be operational noise; three consecutive years of unreversed build creates a stock of soft assets that must eventually be written down, and the write-down is forced when liquidity is draining.
input_signals.reasoning: This changes the accrual leg from a one-year flow to a cumulative stock, testing whether persistence rather than magnitude is what interacts with fragility, and it addresses the coupling concern differently from Signal 2 since two of the three summed years precede the current cash decline. It is a substantive timing hypothesis rather than a rescaling of the winner.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( ts_sum( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), 3 ), at ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, lt ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualBuildAsCoverageCapacityFades
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(pi, lt), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress ultimately means the earnings stream can no longer service the liability stack; a multi-year decline in pretax income relative to total liabilities marks that erosion of debt-service capacity, and accrual builds occurring during it are most likely to be earnings support rather than genuine growth.
input_signals.reasoning: Every conditioner tested so far is balance-sheet based (cash, leverage, retained earnings, debt maturity); this substitutes a flow-based coverage measure, which is the variable creditors actually monitor and the one that triggers covenant renegotiation. If income-based deterioration conditions the accrual effect as strongly as balance-sheet deterioration, the mechanism generalizes; if not, it localizes the story to liquidity rather than profitability.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( trend( ratio( pi, lt ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualBuildAsDebtOutgrowsRevenue
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(lt, sale), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Solvency is ultimately about whether the business can grow into its obligations, so a multi-year rise in liabilities per dollar of revenue marks a firm losing that race; accrual builds occurring while debt-per-revenue climbs are earnings support for a shrinking commercial base rather than investment in a growing one.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the rank-average ensemble with a single new conditioning concept — revenue-scaled debt burden — that is economically separable from the archived asset-scaled leverage trend, because a firm with stable lt/at but collapsing sales shows nothing on the asset-based measure yet is clearly losing debt-service capacity. It is also distinct from the accepted sales-growth conditioner, which uses a one-year demand shock plus a static leverage level, whereas this measures a persistent three-year deterioration in the debt-to-revenue relationship.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( trend( ratio( lt, sale ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: DeteriorationOnlyBitesWhenAlreadyLevered
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), MUL(RANK(RATIO(lt, at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress level and distress deterioration are not substitutes but complements: losing liquidity is survivable for an unlevered firm and existential for a levered one, so the accrual penalty should be concentrated where a high debt load meets a shrinking cash cushion.
input_signals.reasoning: Levels alone produced zero alpha and deterioration alone produced −3.1%, and the untested economic claim is that the level *gates* the deterioration rather than adding to it — a multiplicative gate, not the rank-average ensemble the critic rejected. If the alpha strengthens, the mechanism is a genuine three-way interaction; if it weakens, we learn deterioration works uniformly across the leverage distribution, which is itself an informative constraint on the story.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), mul( rank( ratio( lt, at ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, lt ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualBuildAsNetLiquidityGapWidens
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), lt), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is cash net of debt that must be repaid within the year: a firm whose cash minus short-term debt is deteriorating relative to total obligations has no discretionary liquidity left, which is precisely when soft assets must be liquidated or written down.
input_signals.reasoning: Raw cash overstates available liquidity for firms with large maturing balances, so netting current debt out of the cash position is an economically sharper distress state than the archived che/lt drain, not merely a rescaling. It also separates the liquidity story from the maturity-mismatch story tested earlier by putting both elements in one net-position measure.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( sub( che, dlc ), lt ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWhileInterestBearingDebtRises
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Genuine solvency deterioration means taking on more interest-bearing borrowing; a rise in total liabilities driven by payables is itself an accrual event, so the debt-based conditioning should be tested on financial debt alone.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's leverage-trend conditioner uses lt, which contains accounts payable — the same item that enters the accrual leg with the opposite sign — so part of the −2.2% alpha could be an accounting-identity artifact rather than a distress interaction. Restricting the conditioner to dltt + dlc removes that overlap entirely, making this a clean identification test whose failure or success materially changes how we interpret the whole leverage-trend family.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( trend( ratio( add( dltt, dlc ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualBuildAtWorkingCapitalCovenantEdge
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(ABS(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Bank loan agreements routinely impose a current-ratio or minimum-working-capital covenant, so firms whose net working capital sits near zero relative to their obligations are at the covenant edge, where the incentive to inflate receivables and inventory is strongest and the consequence of a reversal — technical default — is most severe.
input_signals.reasoning: Every conditioner tested so far is monotone in distress, but covenant pressure is inherently non-monotone: firms with comfortably positive working capital face no constraint, and deeply negative-working-capital firms have already breached and been renegotiated, so the danger zone is the neighbourhood of zero. Using the absolute distance of net working capital from zero, scaled by total liabilities, gives a genuinely new economic conditioning variable rather than a preprocessing change to an existing signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( abs( ratio( sub( act, lct ), lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AssetSideAccrualsGatedByLeveredDrain
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp), at)), MUL(RANK(RATIO(lt, at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The manipulable, reversal-prone accruals are on the asset side — receivables and inventory the firm chooses to recognize — whereas payables are supplier decisions; isolating the asset side should preserve or strengthen the fragility interaction while removing the accounting overlap with liability-based conditioners.
input_signals.reasoning: The interest-bearing-debt test showed that part of the leverage-trend family may be manufactured by payables entering the accrual leg negatively and lt positively, so the cleanest fix is to remove payables from the accrual leg rather than from the conditioner. Applying this to the archive's best-performing gate structure makes the comparison exact: if the alpha survives, the mechanism is genuine asset-side accrual reversal under fragility; if it collapses, the winner was largely a payables artifact.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), mul( rank( ratio( lt, at ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, lt ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsGatedByRolloverPressureAndDrain
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), MUL(RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What gates the accrual effect is not how much debt a firm owes but how soon it must be repaid: a cash drain is survivable when obligations are long-dated and fatal when a large share matures within the year.
input_signals.reasoning: The winning gate used the leverage level, but leverage and maturity structure are economically distinct constraints and the archive has never compared them inside the same gate architecture. Substituting the short-term share of liabilities for total leverage isolates exactly that question, and because dlc is excluded from the accrual leg by construction there is no payables-style overlap.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), mul( rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, lt ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsAtTheZeroEarningsThreshold
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(ABS(RATIO(pi, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Earnings management is concentrated at the zero-profit threshold, where a small accrual can flip a reported loss into a profit and preserve creditor and market confidence; firms whose pretax income is close to zero relative to their obligations therefore have both the strongest motive and the thinnest margin for error.
input_signals.reasoning: The covenant-edge signal showed that a non-monotone distress conditioner can outperform every monotone one, and the same benchmark-beating logic applies on the income statement rather than the balance sheet, giving a mechanism the archive has not tested. Scaling pretax income by liabilities rather than assets keeps the measure solvency-relative so that "near zero" means near the point where the earnings stream stops covering the debt load.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( abs( ratio( pi, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsAfterARecentEarningsScar
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(TS_MIN(RATIO(ni, at), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that has posted a deep loss in the recent past is fragile even when its current ratios look ordinary — creditors have tightened, auditors are alert, and management is under pressure to demonstrate recovery — so accrual builds occurring in the shadow of that scar are especially likely to be reversal-bound.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's objection was that the covenant-slide conditioner was mechanically induced by the accrual leg itself, since a working-capital build raises net working capital by construction; the worst realized ROA over the past three years cannot be manufactured by this year's balance-sheet build, so the entanglement is removed. It also leaves the crowded "declining X/lt trend" family entirely, introducing a distress-history state rather than another liability-scaled trajectory.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( ts_min( ratio( ni, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualBuildPerDollarOfEquityCushion
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), MAX(ceq, dp)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The economic severity of an accrual build depends on the size of the cushion that would absorb its write-down, so the same build scaled by total assets means something very different for a thickly capitalized firm than for one whose book equity is nearly exhausted.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than crossing an existing leg with an existing gate, this embeds both themes in a single quantity by replacing the conventional asset deflator with the solvency cushion, so the interaction is intrinsic to the measure rather than an imposed product. Flooring the deflator at one year's depreciation keeps it strictly positive for negative-book-equity firms — who would otherwise be sign-flipped into the long leg — and the 1% winsorization controls the remaining small-denominator tail.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), max( ceq, dp ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: AccrualsAtNearZeroProfitability
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(ABS(RATIO(pi, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The loss-avoidance benchmark is defined on profitability itself, so the firms with the strongest incentive to manufacture accruals are those whose pretax income is close to zero relative to their operating scale, regardless of how large their liability stack happens to be.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that scaling pretax income by lt lets a small |pi/lt| arise from a large debt base rather than from proximity to breakeven, which mixes the threshold mechanism with a leverage effect. Rescaling by assets implements the stated hypothesis cleanly and isolates whether the archive's best result came from the zero-earnings threshold or from the leverage embedded in its deflator — an interpretation question that matters more than another new gate.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( abs( ratio( pi, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: BreakevenAccrualsUnderCreditorPressure
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), MUL(RANK(NEG(ABS(RATIO(pi, at)))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Proximity to breakeven creates the opportunity to manage earnings, but leverage creates the motive: an unlevered firm hovering at zero profit has little to defend, whereas a levered one faces covenant tests, rating triggers and refinancing conversations that make crossing into a reported loss expensive.
input_signals.reasoning: The level-gates-change architecture was the archive's most reliable portfolio result (t = −4.10), and the untested economic claim is that leverage also gates the *threshold* mechanism rather than only the deterioration mechanism — motive and opportunity as complements. If the alpha exceeds both parents the interaction is genuinely three-way; if it merely matches them we learn the threshold gate already embeds creditor pressure.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), mul( rank( neg( abs( ratio( pi, at ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualFlowWhenBloatExceedsCushion
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), MAX(ceq, dp))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose accumulated soft operating assets already exceed its book equity cushion cannot absorb a write-down without impairing solvency, so additional accrual building in that state is the most dangerous configuration on the balance sheet.
input_signals.reasoning: The equity-cushion ratio delivered the archive's strongest FMB slope but negligible alpha, the signature of a sound cross-sectional relation whose extreme quintiles are captured by tiny-denominator firms; converting the cushion-relative bloat into a ranked gate on the signed accrual flow preserves the economics while making portfolio formation stable. The deflator is floored at one year's depreciation so negative-book-equity firms sit at the fragile end rather than being sign-flipped into the long leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), max( ceq, dp ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsAtOwnHistoricalLeveragePeak
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(lt, at), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress is firm-specific: a utility at 60% leverage is normal while a software firm at 30% is stressed, so the relevant state is whether the firm sits at the top of its *own* five-year leverage distribution, which marks a regime its managers and creditors treat as abnormal.
input_signals.reasoning: Every leverage gate in the archive is cross-sectional, so structural industry and business-model differences contaminate who gets classified as fragile; a within-firm time-series rank removes all fixed firm and industry effects and identifies stress from the firm's own baseline. It also differs from the archived leverage *trend* because it registers a sustained peak rather than the slope of recent change.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), ts_rank( ratio( lt, at ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWhenDebtOutstripsHardAssetBase
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(lt, dp), 1)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Leverage measured against total assets is contaminated by the very soft assets accruals inflate, so the honest measure of debt capacity exhaustion is liabilities per dollar of hard, depreciating asset base — the collateral creditors can actually seize and redeploy.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the cosmetic industry-rank swap with a diagnostic that separates two specific confounds: lt/at falls mechanically when a firm books soft assets, so the archived gate partially anti-selects the very firms the hypothesis targets, while lt/dp is immune to that channel and simultaneously captures the collateral-quality dimension that varies across asset technologies. If the alpha strengthens relative to the lt/at gate, the winning gate was being diluted by accrual-driven denominator inflation; if it weakens, we learn total-asset leverage was capturing scale rather than collateral, and the winsorized ratio keeps low-depreciation firms from dominating the tail.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), mul( rank( winsor( ratio( lt, dp ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, lt ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWithinOneShockOfALoss
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ABS(pi), VOL(ni, 5)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Proximity to the loss threshold should be measured in units of the firm's own earnings uncertainty: a firm earning a small profit with very stable income is safe, whereas one earning the same profit with volatile income is a single ordinary shock away from a reported loss and has every incentive to build a reserve of accruals now.
input_signals.reasoning: All archived threshold gates deflate pretax income by a balance-sheet scale (assets or liabilities), which conflates proximity to breakeven with firm size and capital structure; dividing by the five-year volatility of net income creates a distance-to-loss statistic directly analogous to distance-to-default and is the economically correct normalization for a threshold mechanism. Coverage will fall because of the five-year window, which must be weighed against any improvement in alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( abs( pi ), vol( ni, 5 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWhenEquityIsFewShocksFromZero
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ceq, VOL(ni, 5)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Solvency risk is the size of the equity cushion relative to the size of the shocks that erode it, so the fragile firms are those whose book equity amounts to only a few years of typical earnings variation — precisely the firms for which a soft-asset write-down is existential.
input_signals.reasoning: Every leverage gate in the archive is a static ratio of two balance-sheet stocks and therefore treats a stable utility and a volatile cyclical with identical leverage as equally fragile, which is economically wrong; scaling the cushion by earnings volatility introduces the risk dimension the archive has never used. It is also structurally different from Signal 2, which measures distance to a reporting threshold rather than distance to insolvency, so the pair separates the earnings-management motive from genuine default risk.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( ceq, vol( ni, 5 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsInOperationallyLeveredDrainingFirms
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), MUL(RANK(RATIO(dp, sale)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Fragility is not only financial: firms carrying heavy fixed capital charges per dollar of revenue cannot shrink costs when demand weakens, so a working-capital build financed out of a draining cash cushion is far more likely to end in write-downs for them than for asset-light firms with flexible cost structures.
input_signals.reasoning: Every gate tested so far measures financial obligations, while operating leverage — the fixed-cost side of distress risk — has never entered, making this the batch's genuinely new economic channel rather than another liability ratio. Depreciation per dollar of sales is the natural fixed-charge intensity measure available in this menu, and pairing it with the established liquidity-drain trigger keeps the comparison to the archived gate clean.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), mul( rank( ratio( dp, sale ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, lt ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualBuildPerDollarOfReportedProfit
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), MAX(ABS(pi), dp)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is how large the accrual build is relative to the profit it is supporting: when a year's working-capital build dwarfs reported pretax income, the earnings number is essentially a bookkeeping residual, and this is automatically most extreme for firms hovering near breakeven.
input_signals.reasoning: Instead of multiplying the archived accrual leg by the archived breakeven gate — which the critic rightly called a mechanical conjunction — this embeds the threshold mechanism inside the deflator, so the interaction is intrinsic to a single quantity and the resulting signal is not a rank-multiplication of two existing series. Flooring the denominator at one year's depreciation and taking absolute pretax income keeps the measure finite and correctly signed for loss-making firms, which is exactly the tail problem that crippled the earlier cushion-deflated ratio.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), max( abs( pi ), dp ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWhenTangibleCushionIsGone
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ceq, SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc))), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The cushion that actually protects creditors is book equity after the soft working-capital assets are written off; firms whose tangible-of-accruals equity is small or negative relative to obligations have no loss absorption left, so any further accrual build is being layered on an already-exhausted balance sheet.
input_signals.reasoning: This changes exactly one thing relative to the archive — the distress state — and it is a state no prior signal contains: equity net of soft assets rather than raw equity, leverage, or cash. Because the deduction of accumulated soft assets from equity is a level while the signal leg is a one-year flow, the two are not mechanically coupled, and unlike the flagged proposal it does not stack an archived gate onto a re-scaled archived leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( ceq, sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ) ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsUnvalidatedByTaxAuthorities
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(txt, MAX(pi, dp)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Tax expense is an independent, costly-to-manipulate validation of reported income, so a firm booking profits while recognizing almost no tax is either running on loss carryforwards or reporting income the tax authorities do not see — and an accrual build in that state is the classic low-quality-earnings configuration.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the two-threshold conjunction the critic rejected and opens the one channel the archive has never used, the tax variable txt, which supplies external corroboration of earnings rather than another liability-scaled balance-sheet ratio and therefore cannot reselect the same small-liability population. Flooring the denominator at annual depreciation makes the effective-tax measure well behaved for loss firms and near-zero-income firms, so the gate is a smooth non-negative intensity that keeps the signed accrual leg's long-short structure intact.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( txt, max( pi, dp ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWhenLastYearsTangibleCushionWasGone
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(LAG(SUB(ceq, SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc))), 1), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The firms most exposed to accrual reversal are those that entered the year with no equity left after soft working capital is written off; measuring that cushion before the current build establishes it as a pre-existing state rather than a consequence of the accrual being tested.
input_signals.reasoning: The tangible-cushion gate produced the archive's best Sharpe, but it subtracts current soft working capital from equity, so this year's accrual build mechanically depresses the cushion and inflates the gate — exactly the coupling that the earlier cash-drain decoupling test was designed to detect. Lagging the cushion by one year breaks the same-year identity while preserving the economics, so a surviving alpha validates the mechanism and a collapse tells the final generation to prefer the breakeven and levered-drain gates instead.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( lag( sub( ceq, sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ) ), 1 ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsAsAssetProductivityCollapses
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(sale, at), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A multi-year decline in sales generated per dollar of assets means the asset base is becoming unproductive — inventory is not moving and receivables are not converting — so accrual builds during that decline represent assets the business can no longer turn into cash.
input_signals.reasoning: Asset turnover is the one classic Altman distress component the archive has never used, and it is conceptually distinct from every gate tested: it measures operational deterioration rather than financing stress, liquidity, or reporting incentives. The three-year trend form is the construction that has repeatedly worked in this archive, and unlike the failed one-year sales-growth conditioner it captures persistent productivity decay rather than a transitory demand shock.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( trend( ratio( sale, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsOfBarelyProfitableFirms
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), MUL(RANK(NEG(ABS(RATIO(pi, lt)))), INDICATOR(pi, 0)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The threshold mechanism is asymmetric: a firm reporting a small profit is one that plausibly managed its way across the zero line, whereas a firm reporting a small loss has already conceded the benchmark and has less to defend, so the accrual penalty should be concentrated on the profitable side of the threshold.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's best signal treats firms symmetrically around zero, but the earnings-management literature's benchmark logic is explicitly one-sided, and testing that asymmetry is a genuine economic claim rather than a rescaling. The indicator zeroes only the loss-making minority, so the surviving continuous variation still populates both extreme quintiles, and a stronger alpha would establish that the archive's threshold result is driven by benchmark-beating rather than by generic proximity to zero income.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), mul( rank( neg( abs( ratio( pi, lt ) ) ) ), indicator( pi, 0 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWhileBorrowingExceedsEarnings
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(lt, 1), at), RATIO(pi, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose liabilities grew by far more than it earned during the year is filling an external funding gap; accrual builds financed by that gap are soft assets purchased with borrowed money rather than with operating profit.
input_signals.reasoning: Every financing gate in the archive measures either the stock of debt, its trend, or its maturity, never the contemporaneous shortfall between what the firm earned and what it borrowed, which is the flow that actually reveals dependence on external capital. Differencing the two asset-scaled quantities creates a single funding-gap measure whose high end contains firms adding obligations while generating little or negative income, a state distinct from both high leverage and low liquidity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( sub( ratio( delta( lt, 1 ), at ), ratio( pi, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWhenDebtIsReclassifiedAsCurrent
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(dltt, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a borrower breaches a covenant, accountants must reclassify long-term debt as currently due, so a year in which short-term debt rises while long-term debt falls by a similar amount is a visible fingerprint of technical default — and accrual builds reported in such a year are the least credible in the cross-section.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the deflator-permutation search the critic rightly rejected and instead targets a discrete distress *event* rather than a continuous state, which no gate in the archive attempts. Differencing the change in short-term debt against the change in long-term debt distinguishes reclassification (the distress fingerprint) from ordinary new short-term borrowing, which the previously tested Δ(dlc/lt) gate conflated, and both components are asset-scaled so no near-zero denominator arises.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( sub( delta( ratio( dlc, at ), 1 ), delta( ratio( dltt, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsInPeerHeavyFixedCostDrainingFirms
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), MUL(RANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dp, sale))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, lt), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cost inflexibility is what makes an accrual build dangerous when liquidity drains, and the relevant measure is capital intensity abnormal for the firm's own industry rather than the industry's baseline production technology.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that a signed industry z-score used multiplicatively flips the accrual ranking for below-peer firms, implying the economically indefensible claim that accrual builds are rewarded in asset-light firms; ranking the industry z-score keeps the gate on the unit interval so the composite remains monotone in fragility. The gate now implements exactly the stated economics — peer-relative fixed-cost burden interacted with a draining cash cushion — while remaining comparable to the archived raw dp/sale version, so the industry-composition question is answered cleanly.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), mul( rank( ind_zscore( ratio( dp, sale ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, lt ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsInChronicallyMarginalFirms
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(NEG(ABS(RATIO(MA(pi, 3), lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year at breakeven can be a transitory shock, whereas three consecutive years of income hovering near zero against a large liability stack describes a zombie firm surviving on creditor forbearance, where accrual management is chronic rather than opportunistic.
input_signals.reasoning: Every threshold gate tested so far uses a one-year snapshot of pretax income, so persistence of marginality — the distinction between a bad year and a structurally non-viable business — has never been examined despite the archive repeatedly showing that multi-year states outperform single-year ones. Smoothing pretax income over three years also removes transitory items that make |pi| a noisy proximity measure, which should sharpen the gate without materially reducing coverage.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( neg( abs( ratio( ma( pi, 3 ), lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AbnormalVersusOwnAccrualNormAtBreakeven
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(SUB(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at), MA(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at), 3))), RANK(NEG(ABS(RATIO(pi, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms differ permanently in how much working capital their business model requires, so the discretionary component is the deviation of this year's build from the firm's own recent norm, and it is that deviation which should reverse when a breakeven firm can no longer carry it.
input_signals.reasoning: Every accrual leg in the archive is a raw cross-sectional level, which conflates a distributor's structurally high working-capital intensity with an opportunistic build; demeaning by the firm's own three-year average removes the firm fixed effect that industry adjustment failed to remove in generation 2. Pairing this cleaner leg with the archive's best gate isolates the leg-side design choice, and if it improves both metrics it identifies within-firm abnormality as the true carrier of the interaction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( sub( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ), ma( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 3 ) ) ), rank( neg( abs( ratio( pi, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWhileFinancialBorrowingExceedsEarnings
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), at), RATIO(pi, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm raising contractual debt far in excess of what it earned is closing an external funding gap on terms that must be serviced, and accrual builds financed out of that gap are soft assets bought with borrowed money.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic identified the exact flaw in the earlier funding-gap gate: Δlt includes the change in payables, which enters the accrual leg with the opposite sign and manufactures a spurious interaction, precisely the contamination the interest-bearing-debt test diagnosed in generation 4. Restricting the borrowing measure to dltt + dlc removes the overlap entirely while preserving the flow-based external-dependence concept, making this the clean version of a gate that already produced −2.5% alpha in contaminated form.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( sub( ratio( delta( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ), at ), ratio( pi, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsDeepInALiquidityDrawdown
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(che, lt), 5), RATIO(che, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What marks a firm as liquidity-stressed is not the direction of this year's cash change but how far its cash cushion has fallen from the best level it has sustained in recent memory, since that peak reveals the buffer the business itself judged necessary.
input_signals.reasoning: Every liquidity gate in the archive is a one-year change or a fitted trend; a drawdown-from-own-peak is a different statistic that registers a firm sitting persistently far below its own operating norm even in a year when cash happens to tick up, and it is scale-free without the small-cap tilt that the volatility-normalized gates suffered. It is not a blend of tested gates — it uses a max operator over the firm's own history that appears nowhere in the archive — and it keeps the depletion economics that has driven the strongest portfolio results.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( sub( ts_max( ratio( che, lt ), 5 ), ratio( che, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWhileStretchingTaxPayments
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(txp, lt), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Taxes owed but unpaid are the one liability a firm cannot negotiate away, so a rising balance of accrued taxes relative to total obligations signals that cash is being conserved at the expense of a non-negotiable creditor — a strain marker that precedes visible default risk.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the only accrual-menu variable never used in the archive, and it enters here as a non-negative distress gate rather than as a signal leg, which resolves the sign inconsistency that made the earlier tax-deferral proposal incoherent: the accrual build supplies the direction and the tax-stretching intensity supplies the conditioning. Because taxes payable are a small, specific liability rather than a scaled aggregate, this gate is essentially uncorrelated with the leverage, cash and breakeven gates already tested, so the result is informative regardless of sign strength.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), rank( delta( ratio( txp, lt ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWithSlowConvertingWorkingCapital
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The danger of a soft-asset build depends on how quickly those assets convert to cash: a firm already carrying many months of sales tied up in receivables and inventory has a slow, congested operating cycle, so an additional build is far more likely to end in markdowns than in collections.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has scaled the soft-asset stock by liabilities and by the equity cushion but never by revenue, and the revenue scaling measures something economically different — the conversion period of the operating cycle rather than solvency coverage — which is the mechanism that determines whether an accrual reverses through cash collection or through write-off. It therefore complements rather than interpolates the tested gates, and using a stock-to-flow ratio avoids both the small-denominator instability of the cushion ratio and the payables contamination of the liability-scaled gates.
